headline: Approved amended data collection assignments and extended sessions to 3 p.m.
summary: Chairman Goodman read an emailed letter from Travis Morgan, a Nashua resident who has slept outside. The letter asks for emergency shelter, housing pathways, and street outreach, plus better coordination among services. The committee also reviewed a survey for agencies and a workplan.
decisions: Approved an amendment to the data collection assignments, by a motion that carried.
Approved passing the data collection assignments, items a through k, by a motion that carried.
Approved extending sessions from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m., by a motion that carried.

HOMELESS SERVICES GAP ANALYSIS COMMITTEE 
 
  NOVEMBER 12, 2026 
 
A meeting of the Homeless Services Gap Analysis Committee was held Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 1:01 
p.m. in the Aldermanic Chamber and duly noticed in two places, including the City’s website, in accordance with 
the requirements of RSA 91-A:2 II. 
 
Let’s start the meeting by taking a roll call attendance.   
 
The roll call was taken with 7 Members of the Homeless Services Gap Analysis Committee present:   
 
Chairman Goodman presided. 
 
Members of the Committee present: Alderman-at-Large Alicia Gregg, Clerk 
 Alderman Thomas Lopez 
 LaTonya Muccioli 
 Megan Caron, Mayor’s Chief of Staff 
 Bobbie Bagley, Public Health Director (via Zoom) 
 Tonia Knisley, Vice-Chairman 
 Jane Goodman, Chairman 
  
Members of the Committee absent:  
 
Also in Attendance:    Jess Connors, Housing Services Officer 
             
 
ROLL CALL 
  
PRELIMINARY REVIEW OF DATA COLLECTED 
 
Chairman Goodman recognized Alderman-at-Large Alicia Gregg. 
 
REMINDER OF OTHER DATA ASSIGNMENTS 
 
 
a. 211 – Jane Goodman 
b. DPW – Alicia Gregg 
c. Fire/EMS – Bobbie Bagley

MOTION BY ALDERMAN GREGG TO PASS ASSIGNMENTS 
MOTION CARRIED 
 
REVIEW LIVED-EXPERIENCE PLAN 
 
Chairman Goodman to read the following email from Travis Morgan: 
 
“A CALL FOR DIGNITY, COORDINATION, AND HUMANITY 
 
To the Members of the Homeless Services Gap Analysis Committee
Homeless Services Gap Analysis Committee – 11/12/2026                                                                                            
Page 2 
   
My name is Travis Morgan. I live in Nashua. I have slept outside in this city. I've watched people I know struggle 
through the same experience. I don't speak to you from a distance, from a report, or from a collection of statistics. 
I speak from lived experience, from conversations with people on the streets, and from seeing firsthand where the 
system works, where it falls short, and where people get lost. 
 
I am asking you to keep one principle at the center of everything you do: 
 
Dignity must come before doctrine, before paperwork, and before policy. 
 
A bed should never be treated as a reward for good behavior. Shelter is not a privilege someone should have to 
earn by proving they are deserving. It is a foundation. Without a safe place to sleep, everything else becomes 
harder. Recovery, mental health, employment, medical care, stability, and even the ability to make it through 
another day all become secondary to the immediate question of survival.  
 
You cannot reasonably expect someone to rebuild their life while they are sp ending every night trying to figure out 
where they can safely close their eyes. 
 
I am asking this committee to pay particular attention to four critical gaps: 
 
1. Emergency Shelter and Cold-Weather Protection 
 
We need emergency shelter that is accessible when people actually need it, especially when temperatures 
become dangerous. The need does not follow office hours, eligibility schedules, or administrative convenience. 
When the cold comes, people need somewhere safe to go. We should not be waiting until s omeone is in crisis, 
injured, or worse before deciding that shelter is necessary. 
 
2. Mental Health and Substance Use Services 
 
We need accessible mental health and substance use support that meets people where they are, rather than 
turning them away because they aren't ready, aren't stable enough, or don't fit a particular program's 
requirements. Readiness is not always something a person arrives with. Sometimes it develops because 
someone finally meets them with patience, consistency, and compassion.  
 
People don't need another door slammed in their face. They need a door that stays open long enough for them to 
walk through it. 
 
3. Real Housing Pathways 
 
We need more than temporary solutions and promises of eventual stability. We need connected pathways tha t 
move people from the street to emergency shelter, from shelter to transitional options, and from transitional 
housing toward permanent, sustainable housing. 
 
A pathway isn't a pathway if it ends halfway through the journey. We have to look at what happen s after the first 
placement, after the first referral, and after the initial assistance runs out. The goal should not simply be to move 
people out of sight. The goal should be to help people move forward. 
 
4. Street Outreach and Human Connection 
 
We need outreach that treats people as neighbors and human beings, not problems to be managed or 
inconveniences to be relocated. Effective outreach requires trust, consistency, patience, and relationships built 
over time. 
 
Sometimes the first meaningful intervention isn't a referral, a form, or a program. Sometimes it's someone 
remembering your name, asking how you're doing, listening without judgment, and showing up again.  
 
And none of these four areas will function properly if the city departments, serv ice providers, nonprofits, 
healthcare organizations, and community resources operate in separate lanes without meaningful communication.  
 
Coordination is not just another bureaucratic term. It is the difference between someone receiving help and 
someone being passed from one organization to another until they give up.
Homeless Services Gap Analysis Committee – 11/12/2026                                                                                            
Page 3 
   
 
We need a system that works together, communicates effectively, identifies gaps, and takes responsibility for 
what happens when someone falls between the cracks. A referral should be the begi nning of a connection, not 
the end of someone's responsibility to help. 
 
I also want to emphasize something about the people this committee is here to serve.  
 
People with lived experience need a seat at the table. 
 
Not simply as statistics. Not as case studies. Not as stories brought out occasionally to make a report more 
compelling. We need meaningful opportunities to participate in the conversations, decisions, and solutions that 
directly affect our lives. 
 
You can study homelessness. You can analyze service gaps. You can measure outcomes and develop 
recommendations. Those things matter. But the people experiencing these realities carry knowledge that cannot 
be fully captured in a spreadsheet. 
 
Listen to them. Include them. Work alongside them. 
 
I carry a lantern, not a throne. I don't believe leadership means standing above people and deciding what is best 
for them. I believe leadership is stewardship, and stewardship means taking responsibility for helping others find 
their way. 
 
The lantern doesn't belong to me. It belongs to everyone willing to help illuminate the path forward.  
 
Nashua doesn't need another conversation about people without housing that happens without those people 
being present. It needs collaboration, accountability, compassion, and solutions built with the community rather 
than simply delivered to it. 
 
I recognize the work this committee has undertaken, and I appreciate the people willing to put time and effort into 
addressing these challenges. 
 
But I ask you to remember that behind every gap in a service system is a human being living with the 
consequences. 
 
Let's build something that recognizes that. 
 
Please don't just study the people you're trying to serve. Invite us to help build the solutions.  
 
Do this with us, not just about us. 
 
Thank you. 
 
— Travis Morgan 
Nashua, New Hampshire”
